extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical mechanics / gravitational theory (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Newtonian propositions and corollaries about perturbations of planetary orbits, nodal/apsidal motions, and attraction of spherical shells and bodies; focused on the mathematical statements about how bodies attract one another and how those attractions scale. Useful for understanding/teaching classical gravitation and the shell theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apsidal progression/regression under perturbations (Corol. 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipseos a corpore P descriptæ axis seu Apsidum linea, quoad motum angularem progreditur & regreditur per vices, sed magis tamen progreditur, & in singulis corporis revolutionibus per excessum progressionis fertur in consequentia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apsidal motion is determined by the composition of the central attractive force and perturbing forces (LM, KL). In quadratures LM adds and tends to cause regression; in conjunction/opposition the different sign of KL produces progression. Magnitude and sign depend on relative sizes of LM and KL and on whether apsides lie near syzygies or quadratures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apsidal variation depends on deviation from inverse-square (Corol. 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apsides progressus vel regressus a decremento vis centripetæ facto in majori vel minori quam duplicata ratione distantiæ SP pendet; maximus ubi proportio vis in Apside summa ad vim in Apside ima maxime recedit a duplicata ratione inversa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the centripetal force deviates from exact inverse-square, apsidal advance/regress is largest; syzygies (where perturbing subtraction is greatest) yield faster apsidal progression, quadratures yield slower regression. Long duration of these differing phases amplifies observable inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of time-varying centripetal action on eccentricity (Corol. 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpus aliquod vi reciproce proportionali quadrato distantiæ suæ a centro, revolveretur ... & mox, in descensu ab Apside summa ... vis illa per accessum perpetuum vis novæ augeretur ... Orbis igitur, accessu hujus vis novæ, fiet magis excentricus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the centripetal force experiences a periodic incremental increase on approach and decreases on recession, the orbit becomes more eccentric; symmetric increases/decreases can offset. Repeated amplification of the increment/decrement ratio will increase eccentricity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation of orbital inclination/latitude by NM and ML (Corol. 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex viribus NM, ML, quæ sunt causa illa tota, vis ML agendo semper secundum planum Orbis PAB, nunquam perturbat motus in latitudinem, quodq; vis NM ubi Nodi sunt in Syzygiis, agendo etiam secundum idem Orbis planum, non perturbat hos motus; ubi vero sunt in Quadraturis eos maxime perturbat ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Component ML (acting in plane) does not change latitude; NM only perturbs latitude significantly in quadratures. Inclination decreases in transit from quadratures to syzygies and increases on return; nodal position relative to octants determines detailed pattern of minima/maxima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nodal recession in quadratures; stationarity in syzygies (Corol. 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nodi igitur in quadraturis constituti perpetuo recedunt, in Syzygiis (ubi motus in latitudinem nil perturbatur) quiescunt; in locis intermediis ... recedunt tardius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nodes located at quadratures retrograde (recede) each revolution; nodes at syzygies are effectively stationary because latitude perturbations vanish there; intermediate node positions show slower recession or apparent stationarity depending on phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbations greater at conjunction than opposition (Corol. 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omnes illi in his Corollariis descripti errores sunt paulo majores in conjunctione Corporum P, Q quam in eorum Oppositione, idq; ob majores vires generantes NM & ML.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the generating perturbing forces NM and ML are larger in conjunction, the induced errors in orbit (apsidal, nodal, inclination) are slightly larger in conjunction than in opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from magnitude of distant body Q when system rotates about Q (Corol. 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cumq; rationes horum Corollariorum non pendeant a magnitudine corporis Q, obtinent præcedentia omnia, ubi corporis Q tanta statuitur magnitudo ut circa ipsum revolvatur corporum duorum S & P Systema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The qualitative forms of the corollaries hold regardless of Q's absolute magnitude provided a suitable reference frame (e.g., S and P revolve about Q); changing Q's magnitude scales the perturbations but preserves their dependence on geometry and relative distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling of distant perturbing forces with Q's absolute force and inverse-cube distance (Corol. 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cum autem vires NM, ML, ubi corpus Q longinquum est, sint quamproxime ut vis QK & ratio PS ad QS conjunctim ... effectus illi omnes ... sint quamproxime in ratione composita ex ratione directa vis absolutæ corporis Q & ratione triplicata inversa distantiæ QS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a distant perturbing body Q, the perturbing terms NM and ML scale approximately as Q's absolute attracting force times PS/QS, giving net perturbation effects proportional to Q's force and inversely to the cube of its distance (and hence related to apparent diameter cubed). Temporal scaling: perturbations vary reciprocally with square of periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity scaling of errors with orbit dimensions and masses (Corol. 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si manentibus Orbium QE & PAB forma, proportionibus & inclinatione ad invicem, mutetur eorum magnitudo, & si corporum Q & S vel maneant vel mutentur vires in data quavis ratione, hæ vires ... agunt semper eodem modo & eadem proportione: necesse est ut similes & proportionales sint effectus omnes & proportionalia effectuum tempora ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If orbital shapes/inclinations are fixed and sizes/masses scale, all linear errors scale like orbital diameters and angular errors and their characteristic times scale like orbital periods; similar systems yield proportional effects and times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability of error estimates between scaled systems (Corol. 16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si dentur Orbium formæ & inclinatio ad invicem, & mutentur utcunq; corporum magnitudines, vires & distantiæ; ex datis erroribus & errorum temporibus in uno Casu colligi possunt errores & errorum tempora in alio quovis, quam proxime...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given one system's errors and periods, one can compute corresponding errors/times in any similar system by scaling radii linearly and periods quadratically (errors linear in radii, angular errors ~ square of period, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of median force LM to QK and to periodic times (Corol. 17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exponatur vis mediocris LM per radium illum PS, & erit hæc ad vim mediocrem QK vel QN ... ut longitudo PS ad longitudinem QS. ... Est autem vis mediocris QN vel QS ... in ratione composita ex ratione radii QS ad radium PS, & ratione duplicata temporis periodici corporis P circum S ad tempus periodicum corporis S circum Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives practical proportional relations to express perturbing mean forces (LM) in terms of geometric ratios PS:QS and the squares of the involved periods—useful for translating between observed periods/distances and perturbing force magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluid annulus (ring) behaves like ensemble of P-like particles (Corol. 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem legibus quibus corpus P circum corpus S revolvitur, fingamus corpora plura fluida circum idem S ad æquales ab ipso distantias moveri; ... Annuli quoq; inclinatio variabitur, & axis ejus singulis revolutionibus oscillabitur ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A continuous fluid ring composed of many elements follows the same perturbation laws as discrete P; nodes quiesce in syzygies, move fastest in quadratures, inclination and axis oscillate and return each revolution except for nodal precession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tidal behavior: syzygies accelerate, quadratures retard (Corol. 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hic liquor per vices acceleratus & retardatus ... in Syzygiis velocior erit, in Quadraturis tardior quam superficies Globi, & sic fluet in alveo refluetq; ad modum Maris. ... Vis ML trahet aquam deorsum in Quadraturis ... & vis KL trahet eandem sursum in Syzygiis ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying the perturbation analysis to a fluid layer on a rotating sphere yields qualitative tidal behavior: rise (or flow toward) at syzygies due to KL, fall at quadratures due to ML, reproducing tidal acceleration/deceleration patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of rigidity on tidal flow and nodal/precessional motions (Corol. 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si annulus jam rigeat & minuatur Globus, cessabit motus fluendi & refluendi; sed Oscillatorius ille inclinationis motus & præcessio Nodorum manebunt. ... Globus homogeneus & perfectus non retinet motus plures distinctos ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making the annulus rigid suppresses fluid flow (tides) but inclination oscillation and nodal precession persist; a homogeneous perfect globe reduces retention of multiple impressed motions and preserves a single uniform rotation about a fixed axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equatorial mass excess drives nodal regression (Corol. 21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eadem ratione qua materia Globi juxta æquatorem redundans efficit ut Nodi regrediant, atq; adeo per hujus incrementum augetur iste regressus, per diminutionem vero diminuitur & per ablationem tollitur; ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess mass near the equator produces nodal regression; increasing that mass increases regression, decreasing/removing it reduces or stops regression. Conversely, mass removal near equator can reverse node motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Node motion diagnoses internal mass distribution (Corol. 22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex motu Nodorum innotescit constitutio Globi. Nimirum si Globus polos eosdem constanter servat & motus fit in antecedentia, materia juxta æquatorem redundat; si in consequentia, deficit. ... Addendo vero alicubi ... materia nova ... polos ejus errare ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurements of nodal/progressive motion allow inference of how mass is distributed inside the globe: homogeneous sphere preserves axis, added local mass causes pole wandering; direction of node motion (prograde/retrograde) indicates relative excess/deficit near equator or poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion about common center of gravity gives more nearly elliptical orbits (Prop. LXVII, Theor. XXVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus exterius Q, circa interiorum P, S commune Gravitatis centrum C ... describit areas temporibus magis proportionales & Orbem ad formam Ellipseos umbilicum in centro eodem habentis magis accedentem, quam circa corpus intimum & maximum S ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When external body Q is referenced to the common centre of gravity C of interior bodies S and P (using radii to C), Q's areas are more nearly proportional to time and the orbit is more nearly an ellipse about C than about any single interior mass; perturbations are minimal when the common center is stationary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation smallest when common centre is at rest; otherwise grows with motion of inner masses (Prop. LXVIII, Theor. XXVIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus exterius Q ... describit areas temporibus magis proportionales, & Orbem ... magis accedentem, si corpus intimum & maximum his attractionibus perinde atq; cætera agitetur, quam si id vel non attractum quiescat ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inner bodies (S and P) interact among themselves and the common centre remains at rest, external body's motion is least perturbed; perturbation increases if the interior motion deviates (e.g., if inner masses are themselves set in motion or not attracted), so using barycentric coordinates gives the simplest elliptical approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass–force proportionality: absolute attractive forces ∝ masses (Prop. LXIX, Theor. XXIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Systemate corporum plurium ... erunt absolutæ corporum trahentium A, B vires ad invicem, ut sunt ipsa corpora A, B, quorum sunt vires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the hypothesis that mutual accelerative attractions follow an inverse-square law, the absolute attractive 'forces' of bodies are proportional to their masses. Corollaries: in such a system individual bodies' absolute attractions are proportional to their masses; more general laws preserving common proportionality follow similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shell theorem — no net interior force from spherical surface (Prop. LXX, Theor. XXX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Sphæræ superficiei puncta singula tendant vires æquales centripetæ decrescentes in duplicata ratione distantiarum a punctis: dico quod corpusculum intra superficiem constitutum his viribus nullam in partem attrahitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thin spherical shell whose surface elements attract with inverse-square dependence produces zero net force on any particle placed anywhere inside the shell (proof by pairing opposite surface elements and cancellation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shell theorem — exterior attraction as if mass concentrated at center (Prop. LXXI, Theor. XXXI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem positis, dico quod corpusculum extra Sphæricam superficiem constitutum attrahitur ad centrum Sphæræ, vi reciproce proportionali quadrato distantiæ suæ ab eodem centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thin spherical shell attracts an external particle exactly as if all its mass were concentrated at the shell's center: the attraction is directed to the centre and varies inversely with the square of the distance to that centre (proved by geometric decomposition into equal surface elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling of attraction with sphere semi-diameter for given distance ratio (Prop. LXXII, Theor. XXXII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Spheræ cujusvis puncta singula tendant vires æquales ... dico quod vis qua corpusculum attrahitur proportionalis erit semi-diametro Sphæræ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two spheres have diameters proportional to their distances from a particle (i.e., distance scales with diameter), then the attractive force on the particle is proportional to the sphere's semi-diameter; used to relate periods and distances for particles orbiting different-sized spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior of a homogeneous solid sphere exerts force ∝ distance from centre (Prop. LXXIII, Theor. XXXIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad sphæræ alicujus datæ puncta singula tendant æquales vires centripetæ decrescentes in duplicata ratione distantiarum a punctis: dico quod corpusculum intra Sphæram constitutum attrahitur vi proportionali distantiæ suæ ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The net attraction inside a homogeneous solid sphere towards its centre is proportional to the radial distance from the centre (i.e., interior points experience a linear restoring force leading to simple harmonic motion about the centre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exterior of a homogeneous sphere attracts by inverse-square (Prop. LXXIV, Theor. XXXIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem positis, dico quod corpusculum extra Sphæram constitutum attrahitur vi reciproce proportionali quadrato distantiæ suæ ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A homogeneous solid sphere, for external points, attracts as a point mass at its centre with force ∝ 1/(distance^2). This follows by decomposing the sphere into concentric shells and applying the shell result for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual attraction of similar spheres ∝ inverse-square of centre distance (Prop. LXXV, Theor. XXXV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Sphæræ datæ puncta singula tendant vires æquales centripetæ ... dico quod Sphæra quævis alia similaris attrahitur vi reciproce proportionali quadrato distantiæ centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two similar (geometrically similar, homogeneously attractive) spheres attract each other in proportion to 1/(distance between centres)^2; corollaries show how attraction scales with sphere sizes (diameters/volumes) and reduce to point-mass law when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: General concentric-layer spheres: net attraction ∝ inverse-square (Prop. LXXVI, Theor. XXXVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Sphæræ in progressu a centro ad circumferentiam ... dissimilares, in progressu vero per circuitum ad datam omnem a centro distantiam sunt undiq; similares, & vis attractiva puncti cujusq; decrescit in duplicata ratione distantiæ ... dico quod vis tota qua hujusmodi Sphæra una attrahit aliam sit reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even for spheres whose density and attractive power vary radially (but where at each given radius concentric layers are similar), the net attraction between two such spheres behaves as inverse-square with centre distance—proved by composing spheres from concentric similar shells and summing their contributions.
